Thus far

  • Every week so far has targeted one number: the average treatment effect \(\tau = E[Y(1) - Y(0)]\)
  • Design-based inference: randomisation identifies it without a model
  • Covariate adjustment, balancing weights, double robustness: three routes to a better estimate of the same average

But what if treatment effects vary?

  • Medical treatments: some patients benefit, others don’t (or are harmed)
  • Policy interventions: context matters for effectiveness
  • Marketing: not all customers respond the same way

Goal today: understand why estimating heterogeneous effects is fundamentally harder than it seems, and where the ideas for doing it better come from.

(Holland 1986)

The Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference

For any individual unit \(i\), we can never observe both \(Y_i(1)\) and \(Y_i(0)\) simultaneously.

  • Each unit has two potential outcomes: \(Y_i(1)\) and \(Y_i(0)\)
  • We only observe: \(Y_i = A_i Y_i(1) + (1-A_i) Y_i(0)\)
  • The individual treatment effect \(\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\) is fundamentally unobservable

Why it’s fundamental:

  • Not a sample size problem (more data doesn’t help)
  • Not a measurement problem (we can’t measure what doesn’t exist in our world)
  • It’s a metaphysical constraint on what we can learn from data

Implications:

  • We can make causal claims about populations or subgroups
  • We cannot make causal claims about specific individuals with certainty
  • All individual-level causal predictions are inherently model-dependent

What can we learn about individuals?

What we cannot identify:

  • Individual treatment effect: \(\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\)
  • Whether a specific person benefited from treatment

What we can identify (under assumptions):

  • Average Treatment Effect: \(\tau = E[Y(1) - Y(0)]\)
  • Conditional Average Treatment Effect: \(\tau(x) = E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = x]\)

CATE as a compromise:

\[\tau(x) = E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = x]\]

  • Not about individuals, but about groups defined by \(X\)
  • As \(X\) becomes more detailed, groups become smaller
  • But we still need multiple units with similar \(X\) to estimate \(\tau(x)\)
  • Bias-variance tradeoff: more granular \(X\) means smaller groups, higher variance

The role of randomization

For the ATE, randomization is powerful:

  • Ensures \(A \perp (Y(1), Y(0))\)
  • Simple difference in means is unbiased: \(E[\bar{Y}_{A=1} - \bar{Y}_{A=0}] = \tau\)
  • No modeling assumptions needed

For HTEs, randomization helps less:

  • Still have \(A \perp (Y(1), Y(0)) \mid X\)
  • But now we need sufficient treated and control units at each value of \(X\)
  • As the dimension of \(X\) grows, randomization provides less “insurance”
  • We’re back to needing models to extrapolate across covariate space

The curse of dimensionality:

  • With 10 binary covariates: \(2^{10} = 1024\) subgroups
  • Even in a large RCT, many subgroups may have no treated or control units
  • Must borrow strength across subgroups (i.e., model)

How can we do machine learning?

The standard supervised learning paradigm:

  1. Observe many examples of \((X_i, Y_i)\)
  2. Learn function \(f: X \to Y\) that minimizes prediction error
  3. Validate on held-out test set
  4. If test error is low, we trust the model

The temptation:

  • Input: covariates \(X\)
  • Output: treatment effect \(\tau(x)\)
  • Just use your favorite ML algorithm on observed \((X_i, A_i, Y_i)\)!

Why this fails for HTE:

  • No observed target: we never see \(\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\)
  • No natural loss function: can’t compute \((\hat{\tau}(X_i) - \tau_i)^2\) to optimize
  • Validation is impossible: can’t check if predictions are good on a test set

The problem with naive approaches

Consider the naive “difference in predictions” approach (T-learner):

  1. Train \(\hat{\mu}_1(x)\) to predict \(Y\) among treated units
  2. Train \(\hat{\mu}_0(x)\) to predict \(Y\) among control units
  3. Estimate \(\hat{\tau}(x) = \hat{\mu}_1(x) - \hat{\mu}_0(x)\)

(S-learner: train \(\hat{\mu}(a, x)\) by predicting \(Y\) with \((A, X)\) on all data)

This conflates two distinct concepts:

  • Prognostic variables: \(X\) predicts \(Y\) regardless of treatment (baseline risk)
  • Effect moderators: \(X\) modifies the treatment effect

The consequence: overfitting to noise in the heterogeneity, mistaking prognostic variables for moderators, and overconfident, miscalibrated predictions.

What we need: methods that explicitly target \(\tau(x)\), not just \(Y\)

Bonus: (Leng and Dimmery 2024)

What can we observe about our HTE estimates?

You ran an RCT, used a sophisticated HTE method and have \(\hat{\tau}(X_i)\) for all units. Are these estimates trustworthy?

Observation: we can observe subgroup average effects. For any subgroup \(S\), the difference in means is unbiased for \(E[\tau \mid X \in S]\). So build the subgroups from \(\hat{\tau}(X_i)\) itself and check whether they deliver what they promise.

Calibration check:

  1. Sort units by \(\hat{\tau}(X_i)\) into quantiles (e.g., deciles)
  2. In each quantile \(q\), compare the predicted effect \(\bar{\hat{\tau}}_q = \frac{1}{n_q}\sum_{i \in q} \hat{\tau}(X_i)\) with the observed one \(\bar{\tau}_q = \bar{Y}_{A=1,q} - \bar{Y}_{A=0,q}\)
  3. Plot predicted vs. observed

Perfect calibration: points lie on the 45-degree line

Calibration in practice

Evidence from large-scale experiments (Facebook, Criteo platforms):

  • Substantial miscalibration: ML-based HTE estimates are often poorly calibrated
  • Range compression: predicted effects are tightly clustered, observed effects are much wider

Why does this happen?

  • Optimization targets prediction of \(Y\), not \(\tau\)
  • Small treatment effects relative to outcome variance
  • Prognostic/predictive confusion amplified by complex models

Bonus: (Arbour, Dimmery, and Rao 2021)

A complementary approach: can we do better if we choose how to assign treatment?

  • Not all units are equally informative about \(\tau(x)\)
    • Units with common covariate values: less valuable (we already have many like them)
    • Units with rare covariate values: more valuable (fill in gaps in covariate space)

Locally balanced assignments:

  • Ensure good balance not just on average, but locally
  • Assignments are well distributed across covariate space

Connection to today’s themes:

  • Design can’t solve the Fundamental Problem
  • But it can make sure you don’t shoot yourself in the foot

Takeaways

  • The Fundamental Problem matters:
    • We can never observe individual treatment effects
    • This makes HTE estimation fundamentally different from supervised learning
    • Standard ML intuitions can mislead us
  • What makes HTE hard:
    • No ground truth for validation
    • Easy to overfit to noise
    • Prognostic vs. predictive confusion
  • Practical implications:
    • Need specialized methods (which students will present today)
    • Need calibration checks when possible
    • Skepticism is warranted for HTE claims

Open questions

  1. Adapting a workhorse: Random forests predict \(Y\) well. Can a forest target \(\tau(x)\) directly, and still deliver valid confidence intervals?
    • Motivates: (Wager and Athey 2018) on causal forests
  2. Combining models: If we already have good outcome models, how should we combine them to get \(\tau(x)\), and when does each recipe win?
    • Motivates: (Künzel et al. 2019) on meta-learners
  3. Double robustness for CATEs: Last week’s machinery hedged between two models for one number. Can it be pointed at \(\tau(x)\), and how fast can we learn it?
    • Motivates: (Kennedy 2020) on the DR-learner
  4. Inference without a target: If \(\tau_i\) is never observed, what can we test about heterogeneity in an RCT with honest inference?
    • Motivates: (Chernozhukov et al. 2025) on generic ML inference

More to read

Paper Why you’d read it
(Athey and Imbens 2019) The review that frames today: the ML toolkit for applied economists, and where its causal uses part ways with prediction.
(Wager and Athey 2018) Causal forests: honest trees (split on one half, estimate on the other) give consistency and asymptotic normality for \(\tau(x)\).
(Künzel et al. 2019) Meta-learners: S-, T- and X-learners as recipes for any base learner. The X-learner wins when the arms are unbalanced.
(Kennedy 2020) The DR-learner: regress a doubly robust pseudo-outcome on \(X\). The error is a product of nuisance errors, as last week.
(Chernozhukov et al. 2025) Generic ML: test for heterogeneity (BLP), sort groups by it (GATES), describe them (CLAN), with valid inference after sample splitting.
(Athey and Imbens 2016); (Athey, Tibshirani, and Wager 2019) The honest causal tree before causal forests, and the general framework (forests for any local moment condition) after.
(Nie and Wager 2021) The R-learner: Robinson’s residual-on-residual regression as a loss for \(\tau(x)\), with quasi-oracle rates.

Deeper dive: (Kennedy 2020)

The DR-learner

  1. Nuisance training: the propensity score \(\hat{e}\) (in an RCT, known) and the regression functions \(\hat{\mu}_1, \hat{\mu}_0\)
  1. Pseudo-outcome: an unbiased estimate of each unit’s treatment effect \[\hat{\varphi} = \frac{A - \hat{e}}{\hat{e}\,(1 - \hat{e})}\,\big(Y - \hat{\mu}_A\big) + \hat{\mu}_1 - \hat{\mu}_0\]
  1. Smooth the pseudo-outcome: regress \(\hat{\varphi}\) on \(X\) with any ML method. The fit is \(\hat{\tau}_{dr}(x)\).
  • Nuisance training and smoothing must be on separate subsamples (cross-fitting); rotate the folds and average.

Why does this work?

  • \(\varphi\) is the uncentred efficient influence function of the ATE: AIPW, pointwise
  • Its conditional mean is the CATE: \(E[\varphi \mid X] = \tau(X)\). Smoothing \(\varphi\) over \(X\) is a regression with the right target.
  • Plugging in \(\hat{e}, \hat{\mu}_a\) adds bias only through the product of their errors: doubly robust at every \(x\).

Kennedy’s simulation: rough \(\mu_a\), flat \(\tau\). Only the plug-in inherits the roughness.

  • Error \(=\) oracle error of regressing the true \(\varphi\) on \(X\), plus \(\hat{b}(x)^2\)
  • Harder than the ATE by a factor growing in \(\dim X\), shrinking in \(\tau\)’s smoothness

\[\hat{b}(x) = E[\hat{\varphi} - \varphi \mid X = x] = (e - \hat{e})\left\{\frac{\mu_1 - \hat{\mu}_1}{\hat{e}} + \frac{\mu_0 - \hat{\mu}_0}{1 - \hat{e}}\right\}\]

Why does it work better than the X-learner?

  • The X-learner doesn’t benefit from convergence in the propensity score

  • In these experiments we know the true propensity score!

  • We’re using our outcome models as a control variate to reduce variance
    • For a stratified second-stage model, this is just AIPW
  • In practice: pseudo-outcomes are noisy (they divide by \(\hat{e}(1 - \hat{e})\)), so clip \(\hat{e}\) and regularise the second stage. In an RCT with known \(e\), \(\hat{b}(x) = 0\) however bad the \(\hat{\mu}_a\) are.
